clue.text: Foolish joke, better on reflection

indicators.note: A reflection shows a thing the wrong way round, so the word beside it is written back to front.

parts.note: to top an offer is to better it, and TOP is turned round here
a crack is a wisecrack or a gag

explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like a comparison and is a verb: to top somebody's bid is to better it. The comma is where the definition stops and the building starts.
explanation.definitionFit: Foolish -> CRACKPOT: used as an adjective it labels a scheme as crazy, the daft-idea sense rather than the noun for a crank.

clue.text: Hearing, once again, trailer being broadcast

indicators.note: Seed is broadcast by being flung wide across a field, and letters thrown about like that land in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is television, a trailer going out on the channels, and the word doing the work is 'broadcast' in its older farming sense of scattering.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearing, once again -> RETRIAL: a hearing is a court's session of a case, and one heard a second time is exactly that.

clue.text: Chest cold carrier passing on bug originally

parts.note: C is the tap abbreviation for cold

indicators.note: passing on means declining to take, so the bug's letter is left out of the carrier word

parts.note: a basket is something to carry things in

indicators.note: originally picks the first letter of the word bug

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: A cold chest, caught from a carrier who passed on a bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passing on' suggests infecting someone, but it means skipping the B of BASKET.
explanation.definitionFit: A casket is a small box or chest for valuables, and also a coffin.

clue.text: Pooh's half-forgotten no good Hum

parts.note: POOH cut down the middle keeps its first two letters
N is the usual short form of no, as on a tick-box form
G is the standard abbreviation for good

explanation.walkthrough: Winnie-the-Pooh composes little songs he calls Hums, which is why the word is capitalised. The definition is the other hum, British slang for a stink.
explanation.definitionFit: Hum -> PONG: in British usage both mean a strong unpleasant smell, and both work as noun or verb.

clue.text: We trade art abroad to stay afloat

indicators.note: Something abroad is away from where it belongs, so these letters turn up anywhere except home.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a gallery keeping itself solvent, and the definition does carry that figurative sense too. The answer is the swimmer's literal version of the same idea.
explanation.definitionFit: stay afloat -> TREAD WATER: the upright paddling that keeps a swimmer's head above the surface, and by extension holding steady without progress.

clue.text: Modest shaded avenue heading South? Quite the reverse

indicators.note: To head somewhere is to travel towards it, which would leave the compass point at the far end as the destination.
It cancels the arrangement just described: whatever was said to come last comes first instead.

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
a mall was originally a tree-lined walk, as with the one running to Buckingham Palace

explanation.walkthrough: Read the wordplay as written and you build MALLS, which fits the enumeration and is wrong. 'Quite the reverse' is the setter telling you to swap the two pieces over.
explanation.definitionFit: Modest -> SMALL: of a sum or a house, modest means not large, so the two words are plain synonyms in the size sense rather than the humility one.

clue.text: Progress at last, a substitute for milk!

definitions.note: The definition is the exclamation mark that closes the clue: printers and journalists have a slang name for that piece of punctuation, and that name is what the grid wants.

indicators.note: What comes at last comes at the end, so only the closing letter of the word before it is taken.

parts.note: the final letter of Progress
a creamer is the powdered whitener people stir into coffee instead of milk

explanation.walkthrough: The clue looks as though it has no definition at all, and the punctuation is it: a screamer is what printers and sub-editors call an exclamation mark.
explanation.definitionFit: ! -> SCREAMER: the trade nickname for the exclamation mark, from the way it makes a line of type shout.

clue.text: Italian football manager during final leg, riled

indicators.note: Whatever happens during a stretch of time sits inside it, so the letters lie unbroken within the words that follow.

parts.note: seven consecutive letters, starting on the fourth letter of the first word and running through the comma into the last

explanation.walkthrough: Massimiliano Allegri has managed Juventus and Milan, so the definition points at a particular man rather than at a job. A comma is no barrier to a hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian football manager -> ALLEGRI: definition by example, since Allegri is one named Serie A coach rather than a word meaning manager.

clue.text: Fine volley following shot

indicators.note: shot means got rid of, so the letter for following is removed

parts.note: a flight of arrows is a volley of them
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

explanation.surface: A tennis player hits a fine volley after a shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' and 'volley' sound like tennis, but shot means removed and volley is a flight of missiles.
explanation.definitionFit: Light and fine both describe something delicate or thin, as in light rain or fine mist.

clue.text: Grim day to be on lifeboat?

indicators.note: In a down clue one thing sitting on another is directly above it, so the piece named first is written at the top.

parts.note: D is the standard abbreviation for day
Noah's ark carried its passengers safely through the flood

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter's apology for 'lifeboat': an ark rescued everyone aboard, but no lifeboat station would recognise the description.
explanation.definitionFit: Grim -> DARK: of a mood, a joke or a prospect, dark means bleak and forbidding, which is what grim describes.

clue.text: Sinatra when performing, a master of his craft

indicators.note: To perform a piece is to give one arrangement of it, and an arrangement of these letters is exactly what the clue asks for.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'A master of his craft' is exactly what people said about Sinatra, and that is the trap: the phrase is the definition, and the singer is only raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: a master of his craft -> ARTISAN: a skilled hand worker who has learned a trade, so the definition names the man by that mastery.

clue.text: European artist backing commercial noise-reduction system?

indicators.note: A vehicle backing travels in reverse, so the two letters beside it are written the other way round.

parts.note: to plug a product is to give it a free advertisement
RA is the Royal Academician, the crossword's stock artist, and it is reversed here
E is the standard abbreviation for European

explanation.walkthrough: Calling a twist of foam a system is the joke the question mark flags. RA for artist is worth banking: setters reach for it constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: noise-reduction system -> EARPLUG: the grandeur is the joke, but a plug of wax or foam does reduce noise, with no technology involved.

clue.text: Imperial title periodically at issue between two kings

indicators.note: What is done periodically happens at fixed intervals, so the letters are picked up every second step instead of all of them.

parts.note: K is the king of chess and of cards, the first of the pair

indicators.note: It fixes the position of what has just been picked out: those letters sit in the middle, with a royal abbreviation on either side.

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of the phrase
R is Rex, Latin for king, the other of the pair

explanation.walkthrough: Two kings, two different conventions: chess and cards supply K, while Latin supplies R for Rex, the same R that sits in ER on a British postbox.
explanation.definitionFit: Imperial title -> KAISER: the German emperor's own title, a descendant of Caesar, so it names a rank an empire really used.

clue.text: During dry spell, love going for a drink

indicators.note: It puts the swap inside the word rather than at either end, so the change happens in the middle of what follows.
One thing going for another steps aside and lets it have the same place, which is an exchange rather than a straight removal.

parts.note: a drought is a long spell without rain
love is nothing in tennis, written as O, and it is the letter that leaves
the letter that moves into the vacated place

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has love going out for a drink during a dry spell, and it is all decoy: the drink is the definition and the dry spell is a word to be tampered with.
explanation.definitionFit: drink -> DRAUGHT: a draught is one long pull at a glass, as in a draught of ale, so it is a drink in the countable sense.

clue.text: In which salaried English women might be dressed?

definitions.text: In which salaried English women might be dressed

indicators.note: A dressed salad or a dressed shop window has been arranged into a new shape, so the letters are set out afresh.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
E is the standard abbreviation for English
W is the abbreviation for women, as on a changing-room door

explanation.walkthrough: Every word does two jobs at once: read straight the sentence describes the clothes, and read again it hands over the letters. That is what an all-in-one clue is.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue describes the shop department selling clothes for women, which is precisely what such women might be dressed in.

clue.text: Central Line stops bland

indicators.note: To stop a hole or a pipe is to fill it up, so the letter named is pushed into the gap in the other piece.

parts.note: mid means central, as in mid-morning
L is the standard abbreviation for line

explanation.walkthrough: The Central Line is a London Underground route, so the capital letter and the surface both push you towards stations. The printer supplies that red herring free.
explanation.definitionFit: bland -> MILD: of food or flavour, mild means gentle and unassertive, which is what calling a curry bland says about it.

clue.text: Mush something to chew over

indicators.note: Turning something over flips it end for end, so the word it applies to is written the other way round.

parts.note: gum is the stuff people chew for hours and never swallow

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mush' is British slang for the face, as in 'shut your mush'. That is the sense wanted, not anything sloppy in a bowl.
explanation.definitionFit: Mush -> MUG: both are slang for a person's face, the one you are told to shut and the one that ends up in a police photograph.

clue.text: Stirring tonic essentially into a weak gin cocktail

indicators.note: A cocktail is several things shaken together until none of them can be told apart, which is what becomes of these letters.
The essence of a word is its core, so what is wanted is the single character standing at its centre.

parts.note: the middle letter of tonic
anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stirring' is the definition and looks exactly like the instruction; the word that actually mixes is 'cocktail', sitting innocently at the end of a drinks order.
explanation.definitionFit: Stirring -> AWAKENING: as nouns both name the moment something comes to life, so a first stir of interest is a first awakening of it.

clue.text: Taking regular breaks, group stop to plunder

indicators.note: The breaks are the letters skipped and they are all the same size, so walk the words in threes and keep the one you land on.

parts.note: GROUPSTOP falls into GRO, UPS and TOP, and the letter kept is the one each trio starts with

explanation.walkthrough: Nine letters, three kept. The phrase is chosen because it divides exactly into three threes, which is the tell that a counting instruction is in play.
explanation.definitionFit: plunder -> GUT: to gut a shop or a house is to strip everything out of it, which is what a plundering army does.

clue.text: Lead batsman to become established

parts.note: to take somebody somewhere is to lead them there
Joe Root, the England batsman and former Test captain

explanation.walkthrough: Joe Root is an England cricketer, which lets 'Lead batsman' read as a job description on the surface while it is really two separate pieces of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: become established -> TAKE ROOT: a seedling that takes root is fixed in the soil for good, and ideas and rumours borrow the phrase.

clue.text: New Yorker bought cured meat item when reduced

parts.note: got is what you did if you bought something
ham is the salted and cured leg of pork
item cut short loses its closing M

explanation.walkthrough: Gotham has been a nickname for New York since Washington Irving used it in 1807, a long time before Batman borrowed the name for a darker city.
explanation.definitionFit: New Yorker -> GOTHAMITE: Gotham is the city's old nickname, and the -ite ending turns any place name into a word for its inhabitant.

clue.text: Scotch barely open, flipping rubbish party folds

indicators.note: folds means encloses, so the outer pieces wrap the bared letters
flipping means turning over, so the word for rubbish runs backwards

parts.note: rot means rubbish or nonsense
a do is a party

indicators.note: barely means stripped bare, so open loses its outer letters

parts.note: its middle letters

explanation.surface: A barely opened bottle of Scotch is flipped over as the party wraps up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scotch' is a verb, to thwart; TOR and DO fold around PE, the bare middle of open.
explanation.definitionFit: To torpedo a plan is to wreck it, just as to scotch one is to put an end to it.

clue.text: Whisky makers: Ardbeg, Laphroaig and Talisker for starters

indicators.note: For starters means to begin with, so each name in the list gives up only the character it begins with.

parts.note: the opening letter of the four names, with the linking 'and' passed over

explanation.walkthrough: Ardbeg, Laphroaig and Talisker are Scottish distilleries, two on Islay and one on Skye, so the list is genuine and the initials are the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Whisky -> MALT: a malt is whisky made from malted barley alone, so the general word defines this particular kind of it.

clue.text: Switch on air-conditioning, worried about temperature you said?

indicators.note: about means the outer pieces go around the inner ones

parts.note: ate, as in what's eating you, means worried

indicators.note: said means the word you is taken by its sound alone

parts.note: you, spoken aloud, is the name of a letter

explanation.surface: Someone frets about the temperature and asks whether to turn on the air-conditioning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' gives ATE, as in 'what's eating you?'; T and U go inside AC plus ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To actuate a device is to set it working, the same as to switch it on.

clue.text: Red spirit, say, turning up rarely at first

indicators.note: In a down entry, turning something up writes it from the bottom of the grid towards the top, so its two letters change places.

parts.note: gin is the distilled spirit, not the ghostly kind
'say' is eg, meaning for example, written upwards here

indicators.note: At first means at the start, so only the opening character of the word beside it is taken.

parts.note: the first letter of rarely

explanation.walkthrough: Watch 'say': here it is the two-letter eg rather than an instruction to the solver, and it has to be read up the column before it fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Red -> GINGER: ginger is the word English keeps for red hair and for a red-haired cat, so it names that shade exactly.

clue.text: Sierra Grande, ground which could produce vegetables?

definitions.note: The definition describes the answer rather than replacing it: what is wanted is a plural noun for places which could produce vegetables, and the question mark marks that looseness.

indicators.note: Ground is the past tense of grind, and anything ground has been crushed to bits and comes out in a quite different order.

parts.note: Sierra is S in the radio alphabet
anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' wants to belong to the definition, as earth that grows vegetables, and it is the signal to crush the letters instead. Sierra Grande is a real Argentine town.
explanation.definitionFit: which could produce vegetables -> GARDENS: a garden is cultivated ground, and the vegetable plot is one of the main things one is for.

clue.text: Under gravity, form striking carbon crystal

indicators.note: under in a down clue puts the rest below the gravity letter

parts.note: G is the physics symbol for gravity

indicators.note: striking means striking out, so the carbon letter is removed

parts.note: a form is a school class
C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.surface: A striking carbon crystal takes shape under gravity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'striking' looks like an adjective for the crystal, but it deletes C from CLASS.
explanation.definitionFit: Crystal is fine, clear glass, as in crystal decanters and goblets.

clue.text: Resentful canine perhaps time will break

indicators.note: Perhaps flags an example: the word next to it is only one instance of the wider thing the letters actually spell.
To break in is to force a way inside, so the letter arrives in the middle of the other piece rather than at either end.

parts.note: a canine is the tooth that does the biting, one example of the general word
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a dog nursing a grudge. 'Canine perhaps' is the example marker doing its job: you want the general word for what a canine is.
explanation.definitionFit: Resentful -> BITTER: of a person, bitter means soured by a wrong and still nursing it, which is the feeling resentment names.

clue.text: Some grasses become hostile if caught

indicators.note: To catch what somebody says is to hear it, so what the grid wants is the sound of the phrase and not its spelling.

parts.note: a people who rise turn on those set over them, which is becoming hostile

explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' is the usual signal for a word buried inside the clue, and here it belongs to the definition instead; the mechanism is a sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Some grasses -> RYES: rye is a cereal grass grown for grain and for pasture, and the plural covers its several varieties.

clue.text: Question dancer's choice of footwear

definitions.meaning: the verb for working information out of somebody by asking and asking
the flat, thin-soled shoe worn for dancing and for school gym

explanation.walkthrough: Two senses of one short word stand side by side with nothing joining them, which is why the clue reads as a single odd remark about a dancer.
explanation.definitionFit: Question is the verb for drawing information out of somebody, while a dancer's shoe is the light flat kind: one word, two senses that never meet.

clue.text: Plant notice: "No men allowed around stores"

indicators.note: Letters written the other way around are read from right to left, so this run doubles back through the clue.
To store something is to keep it whole and hidden somewhere, so the answer sits complete inside the clue's own letters.

parts.note: seven letters running backwards from the start of the last word to the end of the first, straight over the colon and the quotation mark

explanation.walkthrough: The colon and the quotation marks look as though they seal the phrase off from the rest. They are only punctuation, and a hidden run walks through them.
explanation.definitionFit: Plant -> ANEMONE: the windflower of the buttercup family is one straightforward example of the category the definition names.

clue.text: Character completing apprenticeship argued about raise

indicators.note: about means the pooled letters are moved around into a fresh order
the character completing a word is its final letter

parts.note: its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone finishing an apprenticeship argued about getting a pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raise' could be a verb or a noun, and the answer works as both.
explanation.definitionFit: An upgrade is a raise to a higher grade, level or standard.

clue.text: Resolute hawk going after seconds

indicators.note: What goes after something is written behind it, so this piece follows rather than leads.

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for seconds
to hawk goods is to tout them round the streets

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hawk' is the verb, not the bird: to hawk is to peddle wares door to door. 'Seconds' is the clock's, not a second helping.
explanation.definitionFit: Resolute -> STOUT: a stout defence or stout resistance is firm and unyielding, the courage sense rather than the build or the beer.

clue.text: Hack about, left and right, winning hole at last

indicators.note: To win something is to take it, so the letter named beside it is taken into the answer.

parts.note: re means about or concerning, as at the head of a memo
port is the left-hand side of a ship

indicators.note: At last points to the end of the word next to it, so its closing letter is the one wanted.

parts.note: the final letter of hole
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a round of golf and the wordplay is nautical. 'Hack' is Fleet Street's own word for a jobbing journalist, rude and worn with pride.
explanation.definitionFit: Hack -> REPORTER: a hack is a journalist turning out copy to order, so the word names the trade with a shrug of disparagement.
